chapter_title: Event Systems and Custom Event Handling

screens.title: Event Systems and Custom Event Handling
screens.subtitle: How Unity routes UI input, captures pointer events, and builds decoupled custom events

narration.text: In Unity, the EventSystem is the central manager that makes your UI respond to player input. In this lesson we'll learn why the EventSystem is required, how pointer events like click, enter, and exit are implemented with C# interfaces, and how drag-and-drop uses dedicated drag handlers. We'll also explore UnityEvent for publishing game-level signals without tightly coupling systems together. You will see concrete code patterns: a HoverEffect that responds to pointer enter and exit, a DragDropItem that follows the pointer while handling canvas scale, and a GameManager that publishes a UnityEvent for score or health updates. Understanding these pieces matters because UI responsiveness and modular event flows are a foundation for interactive menus, inventories, and HUDs. A common pitfall is missing a Graphic Raycaster or forgetting to set raycast targets, which silently prevents events from firing. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to implement pointer-based interactions, wire drag behavior safely, and design publisher-subscriber flows using UnityEvent. Consider: which UI elements in your current project depend on correct raycasting?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: EventSystem + raycasters dispatch pointer and input events to UI elements; interfaces implement handlers, and UnityEvent enables decoupled custom signaling.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Event Systems Overview
Why the EventSystem matters
A single manager that processes input, performs raycasts, and routes events so UI elements receive pointer data.
Role
Processes input from mouse, touch, keyboard, and controllers and dispatches events to UI elements that implement handlers.
Raycasting
Works with Graphic Raycaster or Physics Raycaster to determine which element is under the pointer before calling handlers.
Focus & Selection
Manages which UI element is selected so keyboard and controller input reach the expected target.

No EventSystem or missing raycasters means UI elements won't respond; images with Raycast Target enabled can unintentionally block events.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you'll recognize the EventSystem's role in processing input and identify which raycaster your Canvas uses. You'll be able to implement pointer interfaces like pointer enter, exit, click, down, and up to create hover and click behaviors. You will also implement drag handlers to build drag-and-drop inventory items that respect the Canvas scale and rendering order. Finally, you'll declare and invoke UnityEvent events and subscribe programmatically, ensuring you remove listeners when objects are destroyed. Each objective is practical: you'll attach a HoverEffect script to a UI Image, implement DragDropItem that handles canvasGroup and anchoredPosition updates, and design a GameManager that broadcasts a UnityEvent for score or health. These are skills you will use directly in menus, HUDs, and gameplay UI. A quick misconception to avoid is assuming events work without a Graphic Raycaster or EventSystem — verify those components before debugging scripts.

keyIdea.title: Goal
keyIdea.text: Implement pointer and drag handlers and use UnityEvent to decouple publishers and subscribers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Checks
screens.subtitle: Concrete skills and why they matter in a game project

narration.text: These objectives map to real project tasks. You will inspect a Canvas and confirm it has a Graphic Raycaster for screen-space UI or a Physics Raycaster for 3D world-space UI, because the wrong raycaster is a common invisible bug. You will implement pointer handlers to provide hover feedback and to log interactions for debugging. For drag-and-drop you will reparent dragged objects to a top-level Canvas or drag layer, set canvasGroup. blocksRaycasts so other UI can receive hits, and update anchoredPosition using the pointer delta adjusted by the Canvas scale factor. For UnityEvent you'll declare, initialize, invoke, and add/remove listeners programmatically to avoid memory leaks. Each objective includes a verification step: run the scene, watch Debug. Log outputs, and toggle Raycast Target on images to confirm event propagation. These checks make sure you not only write code but also validate runtime event flow.

keyIdea.title: Practical check
keyIdea.text: Verification is runtime: use logs and Raycast Target toggles to confirm events flow as expected.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Skills & Checks
Verification steps
  • Confirm EventSystem exists in scene and Canvas has appropriate Raycaster.
  • Attach HoverEffect and observe color changes and Debug.Log messages during pointer enter/exit/click.
  • Drag the item and verify canvasGroup.blocksRaycasts is toggled to allow drop targets to receive events.
  • Publish a UnityEvent and ensure subscribers update UI without direct GameManager references.
Common misconception
Students often assume a missing script causes no events. More often it's the EventSystem or Raycast Target settings. Always inspect the Canvas and the images' Raycast Target before rewriting scripts.
Quick task
Run the scene, hover over the button and click. If nothing happens, check EventSystem and Graphic Raycaster first.

screens.title: EventSystem: definition and runtime role
screens.subtitle: What the EventSystem does and why it's required

narration.text: The EventSystem is a GameObject that centralizes input processing and event dispatch for Unity UI. It performs two essential tasks: first, it gathers input from devices such as mouse, touch, keyboard, and controllers; second, it uses raycasters to determine which UI element the pointer targets and calls the appropriate handler methods on that element. For screen-space UI you rely on a Graphic Raycaster attached to the Canvas; for world-space UI you may use a Physics Raycaster. Without the EventSystem, regular components like Button or Toggle will not respond because there is no manager to route the input. A concrete example: if your menu buttons are unresponsive after loading a scene, verify the EventSystem exists and that your Canvas has a Graphic Raycaster. A typical misconception is to blame the Button script; often the fix is adding a missing EventSystem or disabling an overlapping image's Raycast Target. Key runtime checks: look for an EventSystem GameObject in the hierarchy, verify the Canvas has the correct Raycaster component, and use logs to see which GameObject receives pointer events. Takeaway: EventSystem is the necessary bridge between raw device input and your UI handlers — always confirm its presence before debugging deeper script logic.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: EventSystem collects device input, runs raycasts, and dispatches events to UI elements that implement event interfaces.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › EventSystem Definition
Runtime responsibilities
  • Collect input across devices and normalize pointer data.
  • Execute raycasts using the Canvas's Graphic Raycaster or a Physics Raycaster.
  • Track selection and focus so keyboard/controller input targets the right element.
Concrete example
If your buttons don't respond in a new scene, confirm there is an EventSystem GameObject and that the Canvas includes a Graphic Raycaster. This fixes many silent failures.
Supporting cards
Graphic Raycaster
Used for screen-space Canvas to detect UI under pointer.
Physics Raycaster
Used with world-space UI and 3D colliders for pointer hits.
Raycast Target
Graphic components can block events; disable when decorative.
Key Takeaway

Always verify the EventSystem and proper raycaster before changing UI scripts during debugging.

screens.title: Raycasting and event propagation
screens.subtitle: How a pointer press becomes an event on a UI element

narration.text: Understanding how raycasting works helps you reason about which object receives events. The chain starts with raw input: the pointer position from the mouse or touch. The EventSystem asks the appropriate raycaster to test UI elements at that screen point. The raycaster returns a sorted list of hits; the first valid target typically receives the event. If a graphic has Raycast Target enabled, it can block elements underneath. During propagation, PointerEventData carries useful context—pointer ID, position, button pressed, and the pointerCurrentRaycast result. A common pattern is to use the pointerCurrentRaycast. gameObject in a drag end method to check whether the drop landed over a valid slot. Concrete example: when you press the left mouse button on an inventory icon, the EventSystem initiates a pointer down and then a click if up occurs on the same element. A misconception to avoid is assuming clicks always reach lower layers; any intermediate graphic with raycast enabled will capture the event. Key checks while debugging: inspect the Graphic Raycaster settings, toggle Raycast Target on overlay images, and print eventData. pointerCurrentRaycast. gameObject during handler calls to see hit targets. Reflect: could a decorative panel be blocking your clicks?

keyIdea.title: Flow
keyIdea.text: Pointer position → Raycaster hit tests → Sorted hit list → EventSystem dispatches handler calls; Raycast Targets can block propagation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Raycasting Flow
Numbered raycast steps
1. Input captured: pointer position and button.
2. Raycaster executes hit test against UI elements and colliders.
3. Hits are sorted by depth; top hit is chosen for dispatch.
4. EventSystem dispatches PointerDown/Click or drag handlers using PointerEventData.
Debugging and example
During a drag-and-drop attempt, log eventData.pointerCurrentRaycast.gameObject in OnEndDrag. If it returns a panel you didn't expect, that panel likely has Raycast Target enabled and is blocking the intended drop target.
Check
Toggle Raycast Target on decorative images to allow clicks to pass through to interactive elements beneath.
Key Takeaway

Raycast order and Raycast Target settings determine which element receives events — examine hits to debug unexpected behavior.

narration.text: Pointer events are implemented by C# interfaces in the UnityEngine. EventSystems namespace. Each interface defines a method that Unity calls when the relevant event occurs. For clicks you implement IPointerClickHandler with OnPointerClick(PointerEventData eventData). For hover you implement IPointerEnterHandler and IPointerExitHandler to receive OnPointerEnter and OnPointerExit respectively. IPointerDownHandler and IPointerUpHandler are useful when you need press and release behavior separate from click. The PointerEventData argument contains the pointer position, pointerId for multi-touch, which mouse button was used, and a pointerCurrentRaycast result. A concrete example is a hover tooltip: OnPointerEnter shows the tooltip and OnPointerExit hides it, using the eventData. position to place the tooltip near the pointer. A common misconception is that OnClick covers all interactions — it does not. If you need granular control for press-and-hold or drag initiation, you must implement the press and drag interfaces. Takeaway: map the player interaction you need to the specific interface; don’t rely only on OnClick for nuanced UI behaviors. Pointer event interfaces means use small, focused interfaces to handle precise pointer interactions; pointereventdata provides context for implementation.. In practical terms, ipointerclickhandler, ipointerenterhandler, ipointerexithandler and friends. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interfaces
keyIdea.text: Use small, focused interfaces to handle precise pointer interactions; PointerEventData provides context for implementation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Pointer Interfaces
Common pointer interfaces
IPointerClickHandler
OnPointerClick receives click events when press and release happen on the same element.
IPointerEnterHandler / IPointerExitHandler
OnPointerEnter and OnPointerExit support hover effects and tooltips.
IPointerDownHandler / IPointerUpHandler
For press-and-hold or separate down/up logic, use these handlers.
Concrete example

Use OnPointerEnter to show a tooltip at eventData.position and OnPointerExit to hide it. For mobile, pointer IDs help you track multiple touches.

PointerEventData highlights
  • position: screen point of the pointer.
  • pointerId: useful for multi-touch tracking.
  • button: which mouse button if applicable.
  • pointerCurrentRaycast: which GameObject was hit by raycast.
Misconception: relying only on OnClick misses press-and-hold and hover-driven flows. Use the right interface for the interaction.

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical HoverEffect script that demonstrates pointer interfaces. The script implements IPointerEnterHandler, IPointerExitHandler, and IPointerClickHandler. In Awake we cache the Image component and the original color, which is important so the object can revert after interactions. OnPointerEnter sets a hover color and logs the event; OnPointerExit restores the original color; OnPointerClick sets a click color briefly and uses a small delayed revert to return to hover or original depending on whether the pointer remains over the element. A useful detail is referencing EventSystem. current. currentSelectedGameObject in the revert to decide whether to apply the hover color or the original one. A common error is assuming GetComponent () always succeeds; guard against null and fall back gracefully. Concrete example: attach the script to a Button with an Image component and set hoverColor to yellow and clickColor to red. Run the scene, move the pointer over the button, and click — you should see color transitions and console logs. Misconception: toggling colors alone won't indicate event flow; include Debug. Log calls so you can confirm handlers execute at runtime. Takeaway: caching components and using pointer data and EventSystem checks makes hover behavior predictable across scenes.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Cache components in Awake, implement the specific interface methods, and use Debug.Log to confirm event calls during development.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › HoverEffect Walkthrough
Key code excerpt
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.EventSystems;
using UnityEngine.UI;

public class HoverEffect : MonoBehaviour, IPointerEnterHandler, IPointerExitHandler, IPointerClickHandler
{
    private Image targetImage;
    private Color originalColor;
    public Color hoverColor = Color.yellow;
    public Color clickColor = Color.red;

    void Awake()
    {
        targetImage = GetComponent<Image>();
        if (targetImage != null) originalColor = targetImage.color;
    }

    public void OnPointerEnter(PointerEventData eventData) { /* set hover color and log */ }
    public void OnPointerExit(PointerEventData eventData) { /* revert to original color and log */ }
    public void OnPointerClick(PointerEventData eventData) { /* set click color, log, and revert after delay */ }
}
This excerpt shows the structure: cache the Image, expose colors, and implement three handlers. Add Debug.Log lines to confirm entry points while testing.
Supporting tips
  • Guard GetComponent calls to avoid null references.
  • Use Invoke or a coroutine to revert color after a short delay.
  • Consider selection checks via EventSystem to decide revert color.
Common mistake

Changing color without setting Raycast Target or without Debug.Log hides whether events fired. Always validate the EventSystem and raycasters when behavior is missing.

screens.title: Drag-and-drop interfaces
screens.subtitle: IBeginDragHandler, IDragHandler, IEndDragHandler and the drag lifecycle

narration.text: Drag-and-drop in Unity's UI system is built from three interfaces that map clearly to the drag lifecycle. IBeginDragHandler exposes OnBeginDrag and is called once when the user begins dragging. Use it to create visuals such as a ghost image, set the item to render on top, and modify canvasGroup properties for transparency and raycast behavior. IDragHandler's OnDrag is called continuously while the pointer moves; update the RectTransform. A reliable pattern is to modify the anchoredPosition by the pointer delta scaled by canvas. scaleFactor because pointer deltas are in screen pixels while RectTransform uses local canvas coordinates. IEndDragHandler's OnEndDrag runs once when the drag finishes; finalize the drop by checking eventData. pointerCurrentRaycast. gameObject for a valid drop target. A common mistake is not changing transform parent while dragging: keeping the item under the same parent can cause it to render behind other UI. Concrete example: reparent the dragged object to the root Canvas and call SetAsLastSibling to ensure visibility, and restore its parent after the drag ends if necessary. Takeaway: split responsibilities across begin, drag, and end handlers, and always consider canvas scale and rendering order in your calculations.

keyIdea.title: Drag lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Begin: prepare and reparent; Drag: update anchoredPosition using eventData.delta / canvas.scaleFactor; End: finalize and check drop target.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Drag-and-Drop Lifecycle
Interface responsibilities

IBeginDragHandler: create ghost, set canvasGroup.alpha, blocksRaycasts = false, and reparent to Canvas.

IDragHandler: update rectTransform.anchoredPosition using eventData.delta divided by canvas.scaleFactor to keep motion consistent across resolutions.

IEndDragHandler: restore alpha and blocksRaycasts, check eventData.pointerCurrentRaycast.gameObject for valid drop location and finalize parent or revert.

Analogy
Think of begin as lifting an object, drag as carrying, and end as placing it down in a slot.
Practical checklist
  • Ensure Canvas reference is the parent Canvas for scaleFactor.
  • Add or require a CanvasGroup component to control alpha and blocksRaycasts.
  • Set transform.SetAsLastSibling() to render on top while dragging.
  • Log eventData.pointerCurrentRaycast to verify drop targets at OnEndDrag.
Key Takeaway

Handle parenting, transparency, and canvas scale to make drag feel correct and to ensure drop detection works.

screens.title: DragDropItem script explained
screens.subtitle: A working implementation that respects canvas scale and raycasts

narration.text: This script shows a practical drag-and-drop implementation. In Awake the script caches RectTransform, parent Canvas, and a CanvasGroup. If no CanvasGroup exists, the script adds one so it can modify alpha and blocksRaycasts. OnBeginDrag sets alpha to 0.6, sets blocksRaycasts to false to allow drop targets below to receive pointer hits, reparents to the Canvas, and calls SetAsLastSibling so the dragged item renders on top. OnDrag updates rectTransform. anchoredPosition by adding eventData. delta divided by canvas. scaleFactor; this division keeps pointer motion consistent across different Canvas scalings and resolutions. OnEndDrag restores the alpha and blocksRaycasts, and contains the place where drop logic can check eventData. pointerCurrentRaycast. gameObject — if it is a valid slot, parent the item to that slot. A common mistake is moving transform. position instead of anchoredPosition, which breaks anchoring and layout in UI. Concrete example: create a DraggableItem image with this script attached, assign width and height to 100, and test by dragging over a DropTarget image. If drop detection fails, log pointerCurrentRaycast to confirm which GameObject received the hit. Takeaway: careful handling of parent, canvas scale, and blocksRaycasts yields predictable drag behavior.

keyIdea.title: Implementation
keyIdea.text: Reparent to canvas, set canvasGroup for visuals, and update anchoredPosition using eventData.delta / canvas.scaleFactor.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › DragDropItem Walkthrough
Key code excerpt
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.EventSystems;
using UnityEngine.UI;

public class DragDropItem : MonoBehaviour, IBeginDragHandler, IDragHandler, IEndDragHandler
{
    private RectTransform rectTransform;
    private Canvas canvas;
    private CanvasGroup canvasGroup;

    void Awake()
    {
        rectTransform = GetComponent<RectTransform>();
        canvas = GetComponentInParent<Canvas>();
        canvasGroup = GetComponent<CanvasGroup>() ?? gameObject.AddComponent<CanvasGroup>();
    }

    public void OnBeginDrag(PointerEventData eventData) { /* set alpha, blocksRaycasts false, reparent, SetAsLastSibling */ }
    public void OnDrag(PointerEventData eventData) { rectTransform.anchoredPosition += eventData.delta / canvas.scaleFactor; }
    public void OnEndDrag(PointerEventData eventData) { /* restore alpha, blocksRaycasts true, finalize parent or leave where dropped */ }
}
Note the dependency on canvas.scaleFactor in OnDrag. This keeps drag motion proportional when Canvas uses different render modes or scale settings.
Debug tips
  • Log eventData.delta and canvas.scaleFactor to validate movement math.
  • Log eventData.pointerCurrentRaycast.gameObject in OnEndDrag to inspect drop target hits.
  • If item disappears behind UI, reparent or SetAsLastSibling during begin.
Common error

Using transform.position instead of anchoredPosition breaks layout and can misplace items. Use RectTransform APIs for UI movement.

screens.title: Reparenting and Canvas considerations
screens.subtitle: Why reparenting, CanvasGroup, and scaleFactor matter for UI drag

narration.text: When implementing drag behavior you are manipulating both visual ordering and input handling. Reparenting a dragged item to the root Canvas or a dedicated drag layer ensures it renders on top of other UI. Using transform. SetAsLastSibling during the drag prevents it from being occluded by sibling elements. CanvasGroup lets you adjust alpha for a ghost effect and crucially controls blocksRaycasts; setting blocksRaycasts to false while dragging allows the raycast to pass through the dragged object and hit potential drop targets below. Canvas. scaleFactor matters because pointer deltas are in screen pixels while RectTransform. anchoredPosition is in canvas-local units; dividing eventData. delta by canvas. scaleFactor results in consistent motion across resolutions. A misconception is to create a separate world-space object for a UI drag without handling coordinate conversions; prefer reparenting under the same Canvas to avoid complex transforms. Example scenario: reparenting to the Canvas root, set canvasGroup. alpha = 0.6, canvasGroup. blocksRaycasts = false on begin, and reverse on end — this combination both makes the item visually distinct and enables accurate drop detection. Takeaway: visual layering, raycast pass-through, and proper coordinate scaling are the three pillars of reliable UI dragging.

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Layering via reparenting, pass-through via CanvasGroup.blocksRaycasts, and coordinate correctness via canvas.scaleFactor.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Canvas & Reparenting
Layer & input control
Reparenting to Canvas root ensures top rendering. CanvasGroup.alpha yields a ghost effect. CanvasGroup.blocksRaycasts=false lets raycasts reach underlying targets while dragging.
Mini-code
transform.SetParent(canvas.transform); transform.SetAsLastSibling(); canvasGroup.alpha = 0.6f; canvasGroup.blocksRaycasts = false;
Scale factor detail
When updating anchoredPosition, use eventData.delta divided by canvas.scaleFactor to convert screen pixels into canvas-local movement. This keeps drag speed consistent when Canvas uses different scaling settings.
Key Takeaway

Reparenting, alpha change, and blocksRaycasts together give a reliable visual and interaction experience for dragged UI elements.

screens.title: Custom events with UnityEvent
screens.subtitle: Create serializable events for decoupled communication

narration.text: UnityEvent provides a simple, serializable way to declare custom events that other objects can subscribe to either in the Inspector or from code. Declare a public UnityEvent or UnityEvent field in the publisher script, initialize it in Awake or Start, and call Invoke to broadcast. For example, a GameManager can expose a public UnityEvent OnScoreUpdated. When the score changes the GameManager invokes the event with the new value. Subscriber scripts such as ScoreDisplay can add listeners in Start using AddListener and remove them in OnDestroy with RemoveListener to avoid memory leaks. UnityEvent is especially useful when you want modular systems: the publisher doesn't need direct references to every consumer. A common misconception is treating UnityEvent as a replacement for robust messaging systems; for simple UI and game-state updates it is ideal, but for more complex patterns you may layer it within a larger event architecture. Concrete example: GameManager initializes OnScoreUpdated = new UnityEvent (); then calls OnScoreUpdated. Invoke(newScore). A subscriber with a public GameManager reference calls gameManager. OnScoreUpdated. AddListener(UpdateDisplay) in Start and gameManager. OnScoreUpdated. RemoveListener(UpdateDisplay) in OnDestroy. Takeaway: UnityEvent offers readable, inspector-friendly decoupling — initialize, invoke, add listener, and remove listener cleanly.

keyIdea.title: Custom events
keyIdea.text: Declare UnityEvent<T> on a publisher, initialize it, Invoke when state changes, and add/remove listeners from subscribers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › UnityEvent Basics
Publisher pattern
public class GameManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public UnityEvent OnGameStarted;
    public UnityEvent OnScoreUpdated;

    void Awake()
    {
        OnGameStarted = new UnityEvent();
        OnScoreUpdated = new UnityEvent();
    }

    public void UpdateScore(int newScore) { OnScoreUpdated.Invoke(newScore); }
}
Initialize UnityEvent fields before invoking to avoid null reference errors. Keeping events public lets designers wire listeners in the Inspector as well.
Subscriber pattern
public class UIMessageDisplay : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameManager gameManager;
    void Start() { gameManager.OnScoreUpdated.AddListener(DisplayScoreMessage); }
    void OnDestroy() { gameManager.OnScoreUpdated.RemoveListener(DisplayScoreMessage); }
    void DisplayScoreMessage(int score) { /* update UI */ }
}
Key Takeaway

UnityEvent gives a simple, inspector-friendly publish/subscribe mechanism — remember to remove listeners to prevent memory leaks.

screens.title: Subscribe, invoke, and lifecycle management
screens.subtitle: AddListener, Invoke, RemoveListener and preventing leaks

narration.text: A robust subscriber lifecycle is essential when using UnityEvent. The common pattern is to add listeners in Start or OnEnable and remove them in OnDestroy or OnDisable. Adding in Start ensures the GameObject is ready; removing in OnDestroy ensures a destroyed subscriber doesn't leave a dangling callback. If you fail to remove listeners and the publisher lives longer than the subscriber, callbacks can attempt to call destroyed methods, causing errors or memory leaks. Concrete example: a ScoreDisplay subscribes to gameManager. OnScoreUpdated. AddListener(UpdateDisplay) in Start and calls gameManager. OnScoreUpdated. RemoveListener(UpdateDisplay) in OnDestroy. When invoking, prefer Invoke rather than calling listeners directly because UnityEvent handles both inspector-wired methods and programmatic listeners. For more complex scenarios you might wrap UnityEvent invocations in null checks or conditional logic to avoid invoking when there are no listeners. A common misconception is that AddListener duplicates entries automatically; repeated AddListener calls will add multiple subscriptions if not managed, so guard against double-adding by tracking subscription state or adding in OnEnable paired with RemoveListener in OnDisable. Takeaway: match AddListener with a RemoveListener in the complementary lifecycle method to keep your event system leak-free and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Add listeners on enable/start, remove them on disable/destroy; avoid duplicate subscriptions and memory leaks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Subscribe & Lifecycle
Best-practice steps
  1. Declare and initialize the UnityEvent in Awake or Start.
  2. Add listeners in Start or OnEnable so subscribers are ready.
  3. Remove listeners in OnDestroy or OnDisable to prevent leaks.
  4. Guard against double subscriptions by pairing enable/disable methods.
Debugging tip
If callbacks execute after objects are destroyed, search for missing RemoveListener calls or double subscriptions added in both Awake and Start.
Example lifecycle
void Start() { gameManager.OnScoreUpdated.AddListener(UpdateDisplay); }
void OnDestroy() { gameManager.OnScoreUpdated.RemoveListener(UpdateDisplay); }
Pitfall

Adding a listener in Awake and again in Start will register duplicates. Ensure subscription happens once or remove previous listeners first.

screens.title: Debugging common event issues
screens.subtitle: Missing EventSystem, blocked raycasts, null UnityEvent, and layout mistakes

narration.text: When UI events fail, four root causes appear frequently. First, a missing EventSystem GameObject: without it no UI handlers run. Second, blocked raycasts: Image or Text components with Raycast Target enabled can capture hits meant for elements beneath. Third, uninitialized UnityEvent fields or missing AddListener/RemoveListener pairs can lead to no callbacks or memory leaks. Fourth, incorrect transform updates like using transform. position instead of RectTransform. anchoredPosition will produce incorrect placement and layout issues. For each problem there is a concrete fix: add an EventSystem to the scene, toggle Raycast Target on decorative graphics to let events pass, initialize UnityEvent fields in Awake before invoking, and use RectTransform APIs for UI movement. A diagnostic example: a drag that doesn't detect drop slots — during OnEndDrag log eventData. pointerCurrentRaycast. gameObject; if it reports your own dragged object, blocksRaycasts was not set false. Another example: a subscriber that never receives events — confirm the subscriber called AddListener and that the publisher invoked the event. Takeaway: approach debugging by checking the EventSystem and raycast settings first, then inspect your handlers and UnityEvent lifecycle. Which of these four causes is most likely in your current UI?

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Check EventSystem presence, raycast blocking, UnityEvent initialization, and correct RectTransform usage when events misbehave.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Debugging Events
Problem vs Fix
Missing EventSystem → Add EventSystem GameObject to scene.
Blocked raycasts → Uncheck Raycast Target on decorative graphics.
Uninitialized UnityEvent → Initialize in Awake before invoking.
Wrong transform API → Use RectTransform.anchoredPosition for UI movement.
Diagnostic checks
  • Run and watch Debug.Log messages in handlers to confirm they execute.
  • Print eventData.pointerCurrentRaycast.gameObject in handlers to inspect hits.
  • Temporarily disable suspected blocking graphics and test again.
  • Ensure AddListener/RemoveListener pairs are present and balanced.
Key Takeaway

Start with EventSystem and raycast checks, then verify handler invocation and UnityEvent lifecycle to resolve most UI event bugs.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact concept cards to carry forward

narration.text: These are the core ideas to retain. First, the EventSystem is required to route input through raycasters to UI handlers; always confirm its presence and the Canvas raycaster type. Second, pointer interfaces provide granular control: choose IPointerEnterHandler, IPointerExitHandler, IPointerClickHandler, IPointerDownHandler, or IPointerUpHandler depending on the interaction you need, and rely on PointerEventData for pointer context. Third, UnityEvent offers a simple publish-subscribe mechanism: initialize in Awake, Invoke when state changes, AddListener in Start or OnEnable, and RemoveListener in OnDestroy or OnDisable. Keep these three ideas in mind as you build menus, inventories, and HUDs: correct routing, the right handler, and clean lifecycle management. A short reflective question: Which of these concepts will prevent more bugs in your next UI implementation? Key Concepts — What to remember means eventsystem + right interfaces + unityevent lifecycle = predictable, decoupled ui interactions.. Serializable publisher/subscriber event type — initialize, invoke, add and remove listeners properly.
Summary

Confirm EventSystem and raycasters, use the specific pointer interfaces you need, and manage UnityEvent subscriptions cleanly to build stable UI interactions.

narration.text: As a quick reference, remember these three points. First, raycasts determine which GameObject receives pointer events, so suspect raycast settings when events fail. Second, when implementing drag-and-drop, reparent to the Canvas, set canvasGroup. blocksRaycasts appropriately, and scale pointer deltas by canvas. scaleFactor to preserve correct movement. Third, UnityEvent simplifies decoupled messaging; always initialize events and pair AddListener with RemoveListener. These short rules help you debug faster and design cleaner interactions. Transition to a 7-minute live coding demonstration. Conclude with a 4-minute segment on custom `UnityEvent<T>`: show how to declare, invoke, and subscribe to a `UnityEvent<int>` for a "player health changed" scenario, connecting a `PlayerHealthManager` (publisher) to a `HealthBarUI` (subscriber) script, explaining the benefits of decoupling.
